title: Warning signs
hookLine: beware groups that isolate you, demand money, or forbid questions

cards: What would it take for you to leave a group you loved? It's a strange question to ask on the way in, which is exactly why it's worth asking. A harmful group may not look harmful from the door.
It can look warm. People remember your name. Someone finally seems to understand you.
The trouble, when it comes, comes slowly: a little less time with old friends, a little more money, a little less room to wonder out loud.
Here are three signs that a place of practice has stopped being good for the people in it.

teach.h: ONE: CUT OFF FROM EVERYONE ELSE.
teach.b: The first sign is isolation. A healthy community adds to your life. It doesn't ask you to cut off your family, drop your old friends, or treat everyone outside as a danger.
If a group slowly becomes the only people you're allowed to trust, notice that.

teach.h: TWO: MONEY THAT KEEPS BEING DEMANDED.
teach.b: The second sign is money that keeps being demanded. Asking for giving isn't the warning; communities need support to keep the lights on.
The warning is pressure: escalating fees for the next secret level, guilt when you can't pay, a leader whose comfort grows while the members' shrinks.
The third sign, maybe the clearest, is a ban on questions. Here the old texts side with the asker.
In the Book of Acts, the people of Berea hear Paul preach, and the text praises them because they "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."
They listened gladly, then they checked, and the text calls that noble.

And the First Letter of John tells its readers, "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God." In these texts, testing what you hear is part of faith, not a betrayal of it.
So here's a plain rule of thumb. A good teacher can hear your hardest question without punishing you for it. A good community lets you visit your mother, keep your savings, and leave on good terms.
If any of that is forbidden, a good first step is to talk to someone outside. And if you're ever unsafe or in crisis, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

how: Healthy religious and spiritual communities usually welcome questions, encourage members to keep their families and friendships, and ask for giving without pressure; people who worry about a group often talk it over with someone outside it before deciding what to do.

o: isolation, money pressure and a ban on questions
a group that asks its members for any donation
strict rules about food, dress and daily prayer

p: cut off from family and friends

s: any group that asks for money is a warning sign
asking for giving isn't the warning. the warning is pressure, escalating fees, and guilt when you can't pay.
in Acts, the Bereans are praised for checking what Paul said
they listened gladly, then searched the scriptures daily to see whether those things were so.
harmful groups usually look harmful from the start
they can look warm. the trouble can come slowly.

games.q: you ask a sincere question at your study group, and the leader says doubt like that will hold you back, and suggests you stop seeing friends who 'confuse' you. what do you do?
o: talk it over with someone you trust outside the group.
cut off the friends, as suggested.
games.why: two of the three warning signs at once: a question punished and a push toward isolation. talking to someone outside is a good first step.

practice: Say the three signs slowly, one per breath: cut off, money pressed, questions forbidden.

Then think of any group you belong to, a faith community, a class, a team, a circle of friends, and without judging it, ask: am I free to ask here? Free to see the people I love? Free to say no to giving?

wordCard.voice: Warning signs. Three marks that a group has stopped being good for its people: it isolates, it presses for money, it forbids questions. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Acts 17:11: examining, the word for what the Bereans did with the scriptures.

carryVoice: Your line: free to ask. If something feels wrong, someone you trust outside the group can help. Take care.
